clinicalPearls: Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with hypotonia, delayed motor milestones and predominantly proximal, often static or slowly progressive weakness
Caused most often by variants in the ryanodine receptor gene RYR1, usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern although recessive forms occur
Muscle biopsy hallmark is central, well-demarcated cores running along the length of type 1 fibres that lack oxidative enzyme staining on NADH, SDH and cytochrome oxidase reactions
There is a strong and clinically critical association with susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia, so anaesthetic history is essential
Orthopaedic complications such as congenital hip dislocation, scoliosis and foot deformity are common and may dominate the picture
Bulbar and respiratory involvement is usually milder than in other congenital myopathies but should still be monitored
Creatine kinase is typically normal or only mildly raised, which helps distinguish it from dystrophies
reference.pathophysiology: Central core disease is a congenital myopathy most commonly resulting from variants in RYR1, which encodes the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Abnormal channel function disturbs excitation-contraction coupling and calcium handling, and over time regions of affected fibres lose mitochondria and oxidative enzyme activity, producing the characteristic amorphous central cores. The same channel dysfunction underlies the linked risk of malignant hyperthermia, in which volatile anaesthetics and depolarising muscle relaxants trigger uncontrolled calcium release, hypermetabolism and rhabdomyolysis. Predominant involvement of type 1 fibres accounts for the proximal, often relatively non-progressive weakness.
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with oxidative enzyme histochemistry to demonstrate central cores in type 1 fibres
Targeted or panel genetic testing including RYR1 sequencing and copy-number analysis
Serum creatine kinase, usually normal or mildly elevated
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to exclude neurogenic and other myopathic causes
Baseline and serial respiratory function testing and orthopaedic assessment for scoliosis and hip dysplasia
Contracture/in-vitro contracture testing or genetic counselling regarding malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
redFlags: History of anaesthetic complications or family history of malignant hyperthermia
Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation
Feeding or swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk in infants
reference.prognosis: Weakness is often static or only slowly progressive and many affected individuals achieve independent ambulation, though orthopaedic and, less commonly, respiratory complications may require ongoing management. The dominant lifelong risk is malignant hyperthermia during anaesthesia, which is preventable with appropriate precautions.
pitfalls: Administering triggering anaesthetic agents without recognising malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
Assuming a normal creatine kinase excludes a significant myopathy
Overlooking cores because oxidative enzyme stains were not performed on biopsy
Attributing static weakness purely to an orthopaedic problem and missing the underlying myopathy
references: Emery-Dreifuss / Dubowitz Muscle Disorders in Childhood
management: Strict avoidance of malignant hyperthermia triggers, using a trigger-free anaesthetic technique that omits volatile agents and depolarising muscle relaxants
Malignant hyperthermia alert documentation and ready availability of dantrolene, with active cooling for any crisis
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain strength, mobility and function
Orthopaedic management of scoliosis, congenital hip dislocation and foot deformities
Baseline and serial respiratory function monitoring with support where weakness affects breathing
Genetic counselling and family screening for RYR1 variants, noting predominantly autosomal dominant with rarer recessive inheritance
